author: James Kirchick
title: Moulton Turns to Lava - Commentary Magazine
text:
Politics and flip-flopping go together like an internal combustion engine and oil; the former cannot function without the latter. At some point in their career, all politicians will feel the need to support something they opposed, oppose something they supported, or take a position determined more by situational ethics than long-standing principle. Rare to nonexistent is the officeholder who is 100 percent consistent throughout the duration of his or her career.
Unlike, say, taking your medication, politics depends on compromise. “A foolish consistency is the hobgoblin of little minds,” Ralph Waldo Emerson once said. There exists a spectrum of mental versatility, from the laudable open-mindedness of John Maynard Keynes’s apocryphal “When the facts change, I change my mind” to the tortured indecision of Hamlet to the capricious tweeting of Donald Trump. In this current election cycle, the most craven policy reversals have come courtesy of an excessively ambitious Democratic representative from Massachusetts whose transparently cynical attempt to ingratiate himself with his party’s left wing failed to win him a seat in the U.S. Senate—and in a most embarrassing fashion.
On November 7, 2024, two days after the election that saw Trump regain the presidency, Massachusetts Democrat Seth Moulton said something that, if extensive polling is to be believed, was obvious to most Americans. “Democrats spend way too much time trying not to offend anyone rather than being brutally honest about the challenges many Americans face,” Moulton told the New York Times. “I have two little girls; I don’t want them getting run over on a playing field by a male or formerly male athlete. But as a Democrat, I’m supposed to be afraid to say that.”
Moulton’s comments came on the heels of a Republican spending spree on campaign attack ads lambasting Democrats for their extremism on transgender issues. The most memorable, a spot featuring Kamala Harris cheerily expressing her support for taxpayer-funded sex-change operations for federal prisoners, ended with the killer line “Kamala is for they/them. President Trump is for you.” Republicans spent tens of millions of dollars airing it more than 30,000 times in swing states. It was a good investment: According to a Democratic super PAC, the “they/them” ad was one of the Trump campaign’s most effective, shifting the race 2.7 percent in the president’s favor.
To most Americans, the proposition that natal males ought to be able to participate in girls’ athletics is one of those things that is so foolish as to require no explanation. So are the other major claims of the transgender movement: that natal males should be placed in women’s rape shelters provided they “identify” as a woman, that minors should be provided with puberty blockers and undergo other irreversible medical interventions if they claim to be the opposite sex (or no sex at all, as the faddish identity “nonbinary” offers its narcissistic denizens), and that the state of mind known as “gender identity” should take precedence over the material reality of biology.
When it comes to sexual orientation and gender identity, most Americans adopt an admirable live-and-let-live attitude. The reason the gay-rights movement was so successful was that it convinced the American people that granting gays and lesbians legal equality would not infringe on their own rights. Nor did it propose a fundamental rejection of reality itself. The transgender movement, by contrast, is unsatisfied with freedom and demands control—over the education system, journalism, the medical profession, the entertainment industry, the English language, and much else. Moulton’s courage in being just one of a handful of Democratic elected officials—and from the country’s most liberal state, no less—to speak the obvious truth about this insanity was praiseworthy.
For questioning the transgender movement’s holy grail, Moulton reaped the whirlwind. His campaign manager resigned in protest. The School Committee in Moulton’s hometown of Salem rebuked him. The state’s Democratic governor preposterously claimed that Moulton was “out of step” with most Americans. (An August Pew poll found 73 percent of Americans “uncomfortable” with transgender participation in women’s sports and 66 percent supporting laws to prohibit it.) And yet Moulton refused to back down. “I’ve never had more people, parents and, by the way, a lot of L.G.B.T.Q. community members, reach out to me and say, ‘Thank you for saying this,’” he told the Times a little over a week after his initial comments caused such a stir. “Some of them are just speaking authentically as parents. Some of them believe the trans movement has gone too far. It is imperiling the progress we’ve made.”
Alas, Moulton’s stint as a courageous politician of principle was short-lived. In January 2025, just two months after decrying his party’s dogmatic position on transgender issues, Moulton voted against The Protection of Women and Girls in Sports Act, a Republican-sponsored bill that would block federal funds to schools that allow biological males to play on women’s teams. “While I’m a proud Democrat, I’ve stated my belief that our party has failed to come to the table in good faith to debate an issue on which the vast majority of Americans believe we are out of touch,” he said, in a befuddling statement that made it sound as if he was voting for the bill he had said “nay” to. “We should be able to discuss regulations for trans athletes in competitive sports, while still staunchly defending the rights of transgender Americans to simply exist without fear of danger or oppression.”
The reason for what a seasoned political consultant would call Moulton’s “evolution” on transgender maximalism became clear later that year when, in October, he announced a long-shot bid to unseat Senator Ed Markey, who has served in Congress for half a century. With Massachusetts essentially being a one-party state, where the winner of the Democratic primary is the unofficial winner of the general election, Moulton correctly figured that if he wanted Markey’s seat, he would have to run against him from the left. This would be difficult, however, as the only member of the U.S. Senate more liberal than Markey is his fellow Bay Stater Elizabeth Warren. And so Moulton would have to throw another bone to progressives to prove his leftist bona fides.
The following day, Moulton reached for the easiest option at hand, announcing that he would stop taking donations from the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC) and return the donations he had already received from the pro-Israel group. “I support Israel’s right to exist, but I’ve also never been afraid to disagree openly with AIPAC when I believe they’re wrong,” he said in the classical formulation positing “Israel’s right to exist” as a controversial position that one should be given credit for just for approving. While anti-AIPAC sentiment on the left of the Democratic Party has been stewing for years, Moulton was the first prominent moderate to rebuke the organization in this fashion.
Though Moulton claimed that his break with AIPAC was “a long time coming,” it could not have been that long considering how he had spent the previous months seeking its endorsement. Moulton was responding to the anti-Israel sentiment that has overtaken the Democratic Party since October 7, and he figured that contributing to the AIPAC-bashing would be an easy way to signal his antipathy to the Jewish state. How quickly things had changed in Massachusetts. When, just two days after the massacre, Markey called for a “de-escalation of violence” at a solidarity rally on Boston Common, he faced a chorus of boos. Two years later, Moulton must have looked at that scene and said to himself, “Hold my Sam Adams.”
Moulton soon discovered, however, that his acts of penance were insufficient. In June, spectators at the Boston Pride Parade booed him. At the first Senate debate the following month, he condemned the Supreme Court’s ruling that states can ban biological males from competing in female sports. At the second debate, with polls showing him trailing Markey by double digits, Moulton made a groveling apology to the “trans community feeling the weight and the pain of the Trump administration policies.” He went on: “I deeply recognize your trauma, and I’m sorry if my comments hurt you.” This still wasn’t good enough, and at the third and final debate, he apologized again.
Moulton’s pandering was all to no avail. On primary day, he lost 65 percent to 35 percent. Neither his self-abasement over the transgender issue nor his attacks on the pro-Israel community convinced a sufficient number of Massachusetts Democrats that he shared their beliefs. If anything, he convinced them that the only thing he believes in is himself. On the one hand, it’s a good thing that the voters were able to spot a fraud. Why vote for the imitation left-winger when you can have the original? But it says nothing positive about my home state that there’s little to no room for a moderate Democrat anymore.
Given the ideological U-turns Moulton had to perform just to mount a credible challenge to Markey, and the slim chances of his winning regardless, one wonders why he didn’t opt to keep his safe House seat. That, at least, would have allowed him to maintain his honor. But honor doesn’t count for much in politics these days. Moulton’s attempt to overthrow then–House Speaker Nancy Pelosi in 2019 and his campaign for president the following year were equally if not more quixotic endeavors and suggest a man committed more to a grandiose image of himself than any steadfast principle. American politics is better without him.
